148.title: Ash Wednesday (Genesis 3:19)
148.hook: ashes on the forehead: dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return
148.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics go to church to receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often wearing it through the day, and those old enough fast and abstain from meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ordinary Time, the long season of counted Sundays. Your line was green, growing. Which ordinary task did you do as if it mattered? Day one hundred forty-eight.

One Wednesday in late winter, you start seeing people around town with a dark smudge on their foreheads. The barista. A nurse on her lunch break. A guy on the subway. Someone at work might lean over and say, you've got something on your face. They know. It's on purpose. Catholics aren't required to go to Mass that day, and still the lines form, to hear something people spend a lot of effort not thinking about. Today: Ash Wednesday.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `THEY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, the season that leads to Easter. The ashes traditionally come from burning the palm branches from the previous year's Palm Sunday, so last spring's celebration becomes this spring's dust. The priest, deacon or minister dips a thumb in the ashes and traces a cross on each forehead, saying one of two sentences. One is from the Gospel of Mark: "repent, and believe the gospel." The other is the traditional one. It comes from Genesis, when God speaks to Adam after the fall. In the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In the old Latin: Memento, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Remember, man, that you are dust. That sounds grim at first. But listen to where it comes from. In Genesis, God forms the first human out of the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. Dust isn't an insult. It's what we're made of, and it's what God chose to breathe into. So, as Catholics read it, the ashes say two things at once. You are going to die. And, in the Genesis story, you are dust that God shaped by hand and filled with breath. That's today's line: dust, and loved. Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast on Ash Wednesday, one full meal and two small ones, and everyone fourteen and older skips meat. The day isn't about being morbid. It's about being honest. Life is short, and knowing that plainly can make you kinder, braver, less hurried about things that don't matter. Other Christians keep it too: Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and more.
screen: `LAST YEAR'S PALMS, BURNED.` · `REPENT, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.` · `DUST THAT GOD BREATHED INTO.` · `FASTING, AND NO MEAT.` · then, large: `DUST THOU ART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with your own mortality, kindly. Settle, and breathe. Touch your forehead lightly with your thumb, where the ashes would go. Let yourself think it: one day, I'll die. Don't rush past it, and don't spiral. Just notice. Then feel your breath going in and out, the same breath Genesis says God gave. If you pray, you can say, dust, and loved. If you don't, just let the plain fact make the next hour a little gentler. The bell holds the time.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, a cross of ashes on the forehead, and the words: dust thou art. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Today, because life is short, say one thing you've been saving to someone who should hear it. Day one hundred forty-eight.

149.title: Prayer, fasting, almsgiving (Matthew 6:1–18)
149.hook: Lent's three practices, done in secret
149.howItsDone: In Lent Catholics take up prayer, fasting and almsgiving, often giving up something, adding a practice, and putting what they save into a parish collection box for the poor, given at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, the day of ashes. Your line was dust, and loved. Did you say something you'd been saving? Day one hundred forty-nine.

You've seen it online. Someone posts a photo from the soup kitchen, well lit, with a caption about giving back. Someone else announces they're on day three of a fast. Someone shares that they've been up since five for prayer. None of it is bad. But there's something odd about it too, and Jesus named it long before phones. On Ash Wednesday, the Gospel at Catholic Mass is his answer. It's about three practices, and one condition. Today: almsgiving, and its two companions.
screen: `A WELL-LIT PHOTO OF GIVING.` → `DAY TWELVE OF A FAST.` → `THREE PRACTICES, ONE CONDITION.`

segments.voice: In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew chapter six, Jesus takes the three great religious practices of his own Jewish tradition, giving to the poor, prayer and fasting, and says the same thing about each one: don't do it to be seen. Do it in secret. On giving, in the Douay-Rheims: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." On prayer: "But thou when thou shalt pray, enter into thy chamber, and having shut the door, pray to thy Father in secret." On fasting, he says, wash your face and look normal, so no one can tell. And each time the promise is the same: your Father who sees in secret will repay you. These three became the backbone of Lent. Prayer turns you toward God. Fasting turns you away from your own appetites. And almsgiving turns you toward your neighbor. Take the word. Alms comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleemosyne, which means mercy. Giving alms is doing mercy. And Catholics count more than money here: time, attention, a meal, a visit, patience. Some parishes hand out a small cardboard box at the start of Lent, and families drop in what they save by eating simply, to be given away at Easter. Why secret? Because the moment you do something good in order to be seen, the audience becomes the point. Jesus calls that having your reward already. Done in secret, the good deed stays pointed at God and at the person you're helping. And there's a freedom in it: nobody's watching, so you don't have to perform. Tomorrow, a walk around the church walls.
screen: `THREE PRACTICES, ALL IN SECRET.` · `LEFT HAND, RIGHT HAND.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, ALMSGIVING.` · `ELEEMOSYNE: MERCY.` · then, large: `THY FATHER WHO SEETH IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one of the three for today. Settle, and breathe. Prayer: a few quiet minutes, door shut, nobody told. Fasting: skip one small thing you'd normally have, a snack, a scroll, a second coffee. Almsgiving: one act of mercy nobody will know about, money to someone in need, or time, or a kind word. Choose one. Picture yourself doing it. Now make one more decision: you won't mention it to anyone. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Almsgiving. From the Greek for mercy. Giving to those in need, one of Lent's three practices, done so the left hand doesn't know. Today's word.
Your line: in secret. Today, do your one chosen practice, and then resist the urge to tell anyone. Let it stay secret. Day one hundred forty-nine.

150.title: The Stations of the Cross
150.hook: fourteen stops from condemnation to the tomb
150.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross especially on Fridays in Lent, walking or turning from station to station around the church, with a reading, a reflection and a prayer at each.

segments.voice: Yesterday, almsgiving, and Lent's three practices. Your line was in secret. Did you manage not to tell anyone? Day one hundred fifty.

Fourteen small pictures or carvings hang along the side walls of many Catholic churches, evenly spaced, each with a little cross above it and a Roman numeral underneath. Most weeks nobody pays them much attention. But on Friday evenings in Lent, the lights dim and a small group gathers at the first one. They stand. They kneel. They move to the next. Slowly, the whole group walks the walls of the church, all the way around, until they end at the tomb. Today: the stations.
screen: `FOURTEEN PICTURES ON THE WALLS.` → `FRIDAY EVENINGS IN LENT.` → `ALL THE WAY AROUND.`

segments.voice: The Stations of the Cross, also called the Way of the Cross, are fourteen stops on Jesus's last journey: from Pilate condemning him, through carrying the cross, the crucifixion, and finally his body laid in the tomb. The word station comes from the Latin statio, a standing place, a place where you stop. It started in Jerusalem, where for centuries pilgrims walked the road Christians believed Jesus walked, praying where things happened. That road is called the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrow. Few Christians could travel to Jerusalem, so over the Middle Ages, and especially through the Franciscans, who looked after the holy places, the walk was brought home. Churches set up stopping points so anyone could make the pilgrimage in their own parish. The number fourteen was settled in the eighteenth century. It's honest to say that some stations come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene helping to carry the cross, and Jesus speaking to the women of Jerusalem. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Others come from tradition: Jesus falling three times, meeting his mother on the way, and Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels don't describe those. In 1991, Pope John Paul the Second led a version with stations drawn only from Scripture, and both forms are prayed today. At each station, people often say, we adore you, O Christ, and we praise you, because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world. Then a reading, a reflection, a prayer, and on to the next. The aim is not to watch, but to walk with him.
screen: `FOURTEEN STOPS TO THE TOMB.` · `STATIO: A PLACE TO STOP.` · `JERUSALEM, BROUGHT HOME.` · `SOME FROM GOSPELS, SOME TRADITION.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk slowly and stop three times. If you can, stand up and take a few slow steps across the room. If you can't, do this in your imagination. Settle, and breathe. First stop: Jesus takes up the cross. Pause. Think of something heavy you're carrying. Walk a little. Second stop: Simon helps him. Think of someone who has helped you carry something. Walk a little. Third stop: he meets the women of Jerusalem. Think of someone who is grieving. If you pray, pray at each stop. The bell holds the time.
Stations. From the Latin for a place to stop. Fourteen stops on Jesus's road from condemnation to the tomb, walked around the walls of a church. Today's word.

Your line: walk it with him. Today, when you walk anywhere, stop three times for one breath, and think of someone carrying something heavy. Tomorrow, the three holiest days begin. Day one hundred fifty.

151.title: Holy Thursday
151.hook: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, washing of feet, and the altar stripped bare
151.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday; in many parishes the priest washes the feet of chosen parishioners, and afterward people keep watch in prayer before the Eucharist at a side altar, often called the altar of repose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stations: fourteen stops from the judgment hall to the tomb. Your line was walk it with him. Did you stop at even one? Today that road reaches its last three days. Day one hundred fifty-one.

Thursday evening, the last week before Easter. The parish church fills up for an evening Mass, and something is off. The tabernacle behind the altar stands open, and it's empty. Then the Gloria begins, and the bells ring out: the little altar bells, sometimes the tower bell too, with the organ at full. And then the bells stop. They won't ring again until Saturday night. A little later the priest takes off his outer vestment, ties a towel around his waist, and kneels on the floor in front of a row of people with their shoes off. Today the three holiest days of the Catholic year begin.
screen: `AN EMPTY TABERNACLE.` → `EVERY BELL, THEN SILENCE.` → `A PRIEST WITH A TOWEL.`

segments.voice: Triduum is Latin for three days. The Church keeps everything from Thursday evening to Sunday evening as one single celebration, counted evening to evening. It begins with this evening Mass and ends with evening prayer on Easter Sunday. Tonight is called the Mass of the Lord's Supper. It remembers the last meal Jesus ate with his friends, and Catholics say two gifts were given at that table: the Eucharist, and the priesthood that celebrates it. Then the strange part. In John's Gospel, during that supper, Jesus gets up, takes a towel, and washes his disciples' feet, a servant's job. Peter won't have it. In the Douay-Rheims he says, "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus tells him that unless he is washed, he has no part with him. Afterward Jesus says, "If then I being your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; you also ought to wash one another's feet." In English this night is often called Maundy Thursday, and the name maundy is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, a commandment, from what Jesus says that night: "A new commandment I give unto you." At the end there's no blessing and no dismissal. The priest carries the Eucharist in procession to a side altar while the church sings, and then the main altar is stripped bare: cloths, candles, flowers, all gone. People stay and keep watch, sometimes until midnight, answering the question from the garden: could you not watch one hour?
screen: `TRIDUUM: THREE DAYS, ONE FEAST.` · `THE LAST SUPPER.` · `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.` · `THE ALTAR STRIPPED BARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash something for someone. You'll do the real washing later: a sink of someone else's dishes, a child's hands, a friend's muddy boots, the mug at work that isn't yours. For now, settle and breathe, and picture doing it slowly, the way a servant would, without being thanked. Notice any part of you that says, like Peter, not me, not that. If you pray, you can bring that part to God. If you don't, just stay with the picture of your hands in the water. The bell holds the time.
Triduum. Three days, from Thursday night to Sunday night, kept as one feast of his death and rising. Today's word.
Your line: the three holiest days begin. Today, wash one thing that isn't yours to wash, and don't mention it to anyone. Day one hundred fifty-one.

152.title: Good Friday
152.hook: no Mass anywhere; people come forward to venerate the cross
152.carry: the one day with no mass
152.howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics attend the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, usually in the afternoon: the Passion from John is read, the Church prays the solemn intercessions, and people come forward to venerate the cross; adults also fast and abstain from meat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Triduum: three days kept as one feast, beginning with a towel and a basin. Your line was the three holiest days begin. Did you wash something that wasn't yours? Day one hundred fifty-two.

Three o'clock on a Friday afternoon. The church is bare. The altar has no cloth, no candles, no flowers. The tabernacle is empty and its door hangs open. There's no opening hymn. The priest and the deacon walk in without a word, and then, in front of everyone, they lie face down on the floor, or kneel, and stay there. The whole church is silent with them. It's the strangest entrance of the year, and it happens on the one afternoon when no Mass is said anywhere in the Catholic world. Today: Good Friday.
screen: `THREE O'CLOCK.` → `A BARE CHURCH.` → `FACE DOWN ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Three o'clock because the Gospels say Jesus died at about the ninth hour, mid-afternoon. And no Mass because, by a very old tradition, the Church doesn't celebrate it on this day at all. Holy Saturday stays quiet too, until the vigil after dark. What happens instead is called the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, and it has three parts. First, the word. The whole Passion is read from John's Gospel, often with the congregation speaking the crowd's lines, so everyone has to say crucify him out loud. In John, Jesus's last words are, "It is consummated." Finished, completed, brought to its end. Second, the prayers. The Church prays ten long intercessions, for the Church, for the Pope and the clergy, for the Jewish people, for those who don't believe in God, for leaders, for the suffering. On the day it remembers his death, it prays for the whole world by name. Third, the cross. A wooden cross is carried in or unveiled, and the priest sings three times, in Latin or in the local language, behold the wood of the cross. Then people come forward one by one to venerate it: a bow, a genuflection, a hand on the wood, a kiss. After that, Communion is given from hosts consecrated the night before, and everyone leaves in silence. Catholics also fast today. And the name? Nobody is completely sure why English says good. Most likely it meant holy, an older sense of the word. In German it's the Friday of mourning.
screen: `NO MASS, BY ANCIENT TRADITION.` · `THE PASSION: IT IS CONSUMMATED.` · `PRAYERS FOR THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `BEHOLD THE WOOD OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a quiet hour at three o'clock. You can't give it an hour right now, so give it these two minutes, and plan the rest. Settle, and breathe. Turn off whatever is making noise. Picture a plain wooden cross, and the long line of people walking up to it, one at a time. If you pray, you can bring someone who is suffering with you to the cross in your mind. If you don't, simply keep the silence, as the whole church does today. Then, at three this afternoon, stop again for a few minutes. The bell holds the time.
Good Friday. The day Christians remember the death of Jesus, with no Mass, a long silence, and a line of people at the cross. Today's word.
Your line: the one day with no mass. Today, at three o'clock, or whenever you can, stop for a real stretch of quiet, with no screen. Day one hundred fifty-two.

153.title: The Easter Vigil
153.hook: a fire in the dark, one candle, then the whole church lit, and the ancient Easter song
153.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Easter Vigil after nightfall on Holy Saturday: the new fire and the Easter candle, the Exsultet sung in candlelight, a series of readings, the Gloria and the alleluia returning, and the baptism and confirmation of adults entering the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Friday: a bare church, a long silence, a line of people at the cross. Your line was the one day with no mass. Did you find your quiet at three? Day one hundred fifty-three.

Saturday night, after dark. The church is completely unlit. Everyone is standing outside, or crowded at the back, around a fire burning in a brazier. The priest blesses the fire, then lights one tall candle from it, the Easter candle, marked with a cross, the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, and this year's numbers. A deacon lifts it high and sings, light of Christ. Everyone answers, thanks be to God. The flame goes from that one candle to the next person's small candle, then the next, then hundreds, until the whole dark church is glowing. Then someone steps up beside the big candle and starts to sing.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE DARK.` → `ONE CANDLE: LIGHT OF CHRIST.` → `THEN THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: What they sing is the Exsultet, the Easter Proclamation. It takes its name from its first Latin word, exsultet, let it rejoice: let the angels of heaven rejoice, let the earth be glad, let the Church sing. Nobody knows for sure who wrote it. It is very old, and it's sung, usually by a deacon, alone, in candlelight. It's long, and it has a refrain that keeps coming back like a drumbeat: this is the night. This is the night, it says, when God led Israel out of Egypt through the sea. This is the night the pillar of fire drove out the darkness. This is the night Christ broke the chains of death and rose from the grave. All of it, the sea and the fire and the tomb, gathered into one night. Then comes a startling line. Speaking of Adam's sin, it sings, in Latin, O felix culpa: O happy fault, that earned for us so great a Redeemer. It dares to call the first sin happy, because of where the story went. And, lovely detail: it thanks the bees. The candle is beeswax, and the song praises the work of the mother bee who made it. After the Exsultet come the readings, up to seven from the Old Testament, walking through the whole story from creation. Then the Gloria, every bell ringing again after two days of silence. The alleluia returns. And adults who have been preparing are baptized and confirmed that night. Augustine called this vigil the mother of all vigils.
screen: `EXSULTET: LET IT REJOICE.` · `THIS IS THE NIGHT.` · `O HAPPY FAULT.` · `BELLS, ALLELUIA, BAPTISMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle in the dark. If you can, turn off the lights in your room now, or tonight, and light one candle, or a phone screen turned low if a candle isn't safe. Settle, and breathe. Watch how far one small flame reaches. Notice what it lights and what it doesn't. If you pray, you can say, as the church answers at the vigil, thanks be to God. If you don't, simply watch the light and let the dark around it be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Exsultet. Let it rejoice. The ancient Easter song, sung beside one candle in a dark church. Today's word.
Your line: this is the night. Tonight, when it gets dark, turn on one light slowly, on purpose, and notice the room come back. Day one hundred fifty-three.

154.title: Fifty days of Easter
154.hook: Easter lasts until Pentecost; the alleluia returns
154.tomorrow: Holy days and the saints' calendar
154.howItsDone: Catholics keep Easter as a fifty-day season ending at Pentecost: the Easter candle burns at Mass, the alleluia is sung again, the Regina Caeli replaces the Angelus, and the first eight days are each celebrated like Easter Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exsultet, sung beside one candle in the dark. Your line was this is the night. Did you turn a light on slowly? Today closes the week. Day one hundred fifty-four.

Easter Sunday: the eggs, the lamb, the big lunch, the chocolate, the cousins asleep on the couch. By Monday the decorations are in a box. By Tuesday it's back to normal, and Easter feels like it came and went in a day. Meanwhile the Church is just getting started. For six weeks it gave things up. Now, on the calendar it keeps, the party runs for seven weeks. Today: the fifty days of Easter.
screen: `MONDAY: DECORATIONS IN A BOX.` → `THE CHURCH IS JUST STARTING.`

segments.voice: Easter isn't a day for Catholics. It's a season, fifty days long, from Easter Sunday to Pentecost. It starts with the octave: eight days, each one kept as if it were Easter Sunday itself, with the Gloria every day and a double alleluia at the dismissal. Then the season runs on. On the fortieth day, or where it's moved, the Sunday after, the Church remembers the Ascension, because the Acts of the Apostles says the risen Jesus appeared to his friends over forty days. And on the fiftieth comes Pentecost, which is simply Greek for fiftieth, the day the Holy Spirit came. So the arithmetic is on purpose. Lent is forty days. Easter is fifty. The feast is longer than the fast. And the sound of the season is the word that went missing. All through Lent, Catholics don't say or sing alleluia at Mass. Some old customs even said goodbye to it before Lent, and in a few places, tradition says, people buried a scroll with the word written on it. Now it's back, everywhere, doubled and tripled. Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, and Yah, a short form of God's name. It passed into Greek and Latin untranslated, and it's still said in its original form in churches around the world. A few more things change for fifty days. The tall Easter candle from the vigil is lit at every Mass. At noon, in place of the Angelus, the custom is the Regina Caeli, Queen of Heaven, rejoice. And everything of the last weeks, the ashes, the stations, the towel on Thursday, the fire on Saturday, was pointing here.
screen: `AN OCTAVE: EIGHT EASTER SUNDAYS.` · `FORTY DAYS TO THE ASCENSION.` · `PENTECOST MEANS FIFTIETH.` · `THE ALLELUIA COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say alleluia out loud. Not in your head. Out loud, even quietly, even if it feels odd in your kitchen. Settle first, and breathe. Then say it once, and listen to the sound of it. Say it again, a little slower. Notice what in your life right now is worth praise: one person, one mercy, one ordinary good thing. If you pray, you can offer it to God as a single word. If you don't, let it be a word of gladness. Then sit with the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
Alleluia. Hebrew for praise Yah, the word that disappears for Lent and comes back doubled through the fifty days of Easter. Today's word.
